title: Integral Newton expansion in finitely many variables
statement: For $r,D\in\mathbf N$, let $P\in\mathbf Q[X_1,\ldots,X_r]$ be a polynomial of total degree at most $D$; here $\mathbf Q[X_1,\ldots,X_r]$ is the polynomial ring in $r$ variables [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], and the total degree of a nonzero polynomial is the largest $\sum_i\alpha_i$ of a monomial $X^\alpha$ with nonzero coefficient. For $b=(b_1,\ldots,b_r)\in\mathbf N^r$, set $|b|=\sum_i b_i$ and $B_b(X)=\prod_i\binom{X_i}{b_i}$, where $\binom{X}{j}=X(X-1)\cdots(X-j+1)/j!$ and $\binom{X}{0}=1$. There is a unique expansion $$P=\sum_{|b|\le D}c_b B_b,\qquad c_b\in\mathbf Q.$$ Its coefficients are $c_b=(\Delta_1^{b_1}\cdots\Delta_r^{b_r}P)(0)$, where $\Delta_iP(X)=P(X_1,\ldots,X_i+1,\ldots,X_r)-P(X)$. If $P$ takes integer values on $\mathbf N^r$, every $c_b$ is an integer. Conversely, integer coefficients $c_b$ imply that $P$ takes integer values on $\mathbf Z^r$. In particular every polynomial $\binom{s+\sum_i u_iX_i}{t}$ with $s,u_i\in\mathbf Z$ and $t\in\mathbf N$ is an integer linear combination of the $B_b$ with $|b|\le t$. For $r=0$ these statements mean that a rational constant is integer-valued exactly when it is an integer.

proof.text: Let $V_D$ be the rational span of the monomials $X^b$ with $|b|\le D$. By the polynomial-ring definition those monomials are a basis: polynomial coefficients are unique. This is a finite family since each $b_i\le D$. Expanding the defining product gives $B_b=(\prod_i b_i!)^{-1}X^b+$ terms of strictly smaller total degree; the only way to obtain total degree $|b|$ is to take $X_i$ from every factor. Order the finite indices by total degree, with any order inside equal degrees. The coordinate matrix of the $B_b$ in the monomial basis is triangular, and its diagonal entries $(\prod_i b_i!)^{-1}$ are nonzero rational numbers, hence units. The cited triangular basis-change lemma applies with $R=\mathbf Q$, $F=V_D$ and this finite basis. Thus the $B_b$, $|b|\le D$, form a basis of $V_D$, giving existence and uniqueness of the required expansion.

proof.text: Write $F_j(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{j-1}(X-k)$ and $q_j=F_j/j!$. Directly $q_0=1$, so $\Delta q_0=0$. For $j\ge1$, factor out $F_{j-1}(X)$ to compute $F_j(X+1)-F_j(X)=((X+1)-(X-j+1))F_{j-1}(X)=jF_{j-1}(X)$. Dividing by $j!$ gives $\Delta q_j=q_{j-1}$. Since the other factors in $B_b$ are independent of $X_i$, $\Delta_iB_b=B_{b-e_i}$ if $b_i>0$ and is zero if $b_i=0$. Also $q_j(0)=0$ for $j>0$, and $q_0(0)=1$.

source.place: Stacks Tag 00JX, algebra.tex, definition-numerical-polynomial and the paragraph immediately following it (univariate integral binomial expansion); the stated multivariate degree bound and forward-difference coefficient formula are the supporting extension to commuting Cartan variables.; explicit multivariate argument written by Q35, step 2

proof.text: Translations in different coordinates commute: both orders send $P(X)$ to $P(X+e_i+e_j)$; subtracting shows that the $\Delta_i$ commute too. They are rational-linear. Apply $\Delta_1^{a_1}\cdots\Delta_r^{a_r}$ to the finite expansion from step 1 and evaluate at zero. Repeatedly using step 2, the term indexed by $b$ is zero if any $a_i>b_i$; otherwise it is $B_{b-a}(0)$, which is $1$ precisely for $b=a$ and zero otherwise. Thus the result is $c_a$ for each $|a|\le D$, as claimed.

source.place: Stacks Tag 00JX, algebra.tex, definition-numerical-polynomial and the paragraph immediately following it (univariate integral binomial expansion); the stated multivariate degree bound and forward-difference coefficient formula are the supporting extension to commuting Cartan variables.; explicit multivariate argument written by Q35, step 3

proof.text: If $P$ has integer values on $\mathbf N^r$, each coordinate difference has integer values there: its value at $n$ is the difference of the two integers $P(n+e_i)$ and $P(n)$. Induct on the number of differences, beginning with $P$, to obtain the same assertion for every iterated difference; all shifted points remain in $\mathbf N^r$. Evaluating at zero and using step 3 proves $c_b\in\mathbf Z$.

proof.text: For $z\in\mathbf Z$ and $j\in\mathbf N$, the cited factorial-divisibility statement supplies $a\in\mathbf Z$ with $F_j(z)=j!a$. Cast this equality into $\mathbf Q$ and divide by the nonzero $j!$ to get $q_j(z)=a$. Hence every factor in $B_b(z_1,\ldots,z_r)$ is integral, including negative $z_i$, so the product is integral. If all $c_b$ are integers, their finite linear combination in the expansion is integral at every point of $\mathbf Z^r$.

source.place: Stacks Tag 00JX, algebra.tex, definition-numerical-polynomial and the paragraph immediately following it (univariate integral binomial expansion); the stated multivariate degree bound and forward-difference coefficient formula are the supporting extension to commuting Cartan variables.; explicit multivariate argument written by Q35, step 5

proof.text: Put $L=s+\sum_i u_iX_i$. The product $q_t(L)=\prod_{j=0}^{t-1}(L-j)/t!$ has total degree at most $t$: each factor has degree at most one, and expanding a product of $t$ such factors selects at most $t$ variables in any monomial. At every $n\in\mathbf N^r$, $L(n)$ is an integer even if some $u_i$ or $s$ are negative. Apply the factorial-divisibility statement with $z=L(n)$ to see that $q_t(L(n))$ is an integer. Steps 1 and 4, with $D=t$, therefore give the asserted integral combination with $|b|\le t$.

proof.text: For $r=0$ the only multi-index is the empty tuple, of weight zero, and its product $B_{()}$ is $1$. The unique expansion is the rational constant itself times $1$, and the empty composition of differences is the identity evaluated at the unique empty tuple. The sets $\mathbf N^0$ and $\mathbf Z^0$ are both singletons, so integer-valuedness is exactly integrality of the constant. For $D=0$ in any number of variables the same constant calculation applies. The zero polynomial has all coefficients zero; $t=0$ gives the constant $1$.
